readerContract.humanQuestion: OpenAI says it wants mandatory national AI safety rules, while lawmakers are talking about pausing advanced AI. What is each side actually proposing, and is any of it law?
readerContract.promisedPayoff: Separate a company request from a forthcoming legislative proposal, understand the different triggers each would use, and know what has and has not changed legally.
readerContract.priorKnowledge: No knowledge of Congress, frontier AI, capability thresholds, independent assessments or superintelligence is assumed.
readerContract.centralMentalModel: These are two proposed braking systems: one adds mandatory checks and reporting around the most capable laboratories; the other would stop a broader category of development until a regulator writes rules and permanently ban a defined future category.
readerContract.dailyLifeConnection: Readers encounter headlines saying AI safety rules are coming; the practical job is to tell a company position, an announced bill and an enacted law apart before assuming products or rights changed.
readerContract.surfaceJob: A September 11 NewsStand explanation of OpenAI’s September 9 policy call, with the September 3 Sanders-Casar proposal only as a useful comparison.
readerContract.desiredFeeling: I can explain what each proposal would require, who is asking for it, and why neither announcement changed federal law today.

canonicalTruth.owner: OpenAI owns its policy request; Sanders and Casar own their forthcoming proposal; Reuters owns its independent reporting on the announcement and current federal-framework status; NewsStand owns the bounded comparison.
canonicalTruth.freshnessTrigger: Reopen all sources on publication day; redraft if formal bill text or number appears, Congress advances a federal framework, the White House signs a relevant law, OpenAI changes its requested scope, or credible reporting corrects these descriptions.

draftArchitecture.plainAnswer: On September 9, OpenAI asked Congress for mandatory capability-based rules for the handful of labs building the most capable systems. Sanders and Casar had announced a different, forthcoming proposal: pause advanced AI development until a federal regulator sets rules and permanently ban their defined category of superintelligence. Neither announcement is a new federal law.
causalSequence: OpenAI’s September 9 post asks Congress to replace lab-by-lab voluntary promises with mandatory national requirements.

Its preferred system would apply common testing, independent assessment, cybersecurity and incident-reporting duties to a handful of well-resourced frontier laboratories, with obligations scaling to capability and risk.

The Sanders-Casar September 3 announcement proposes a stronger brake: pause advanced development until a new regulator has rules and a model-review process, while permanently banning the announced category of superintelligence.
The two proposals therefore differ in both coverage and trigger: required evidence while frontier development continues versus a pause before advanced development continues.
Because one is a company request and the other is expressly forthcoming legislation, neither creates a federal legal duty today.
draftArchitecture.workedCase: A headline saying “mandatory rules” can describe what a company wants Congress to enact, while another headline saying lawmakers “introduce” a ban can still point to a sponsor page that calls the text forthcoming. Legal effect depends on the actual status, not the strongest verb in a headline.
draftArchitecture.transferCase: For another policy headline, identify the speaker, the instrument, the covered systems and the trigger before deciding whether anything changed for the public.
draftArchitecture.usefulAction: When a policy headline appears, check whether the source is a company position, announced proposal, formally introduced bill or enacted law; then ask which systems are covered and what event triggers testing, reporting, slowing or stopping.
draftArchitecture.formatSpecificStructure: The Story; LAiDIES Read; What This Means for You; Cocktail Party; Class Notes.
draftArchitecture.antiTemplateDecision: Lead with the legal status and concrete OpenAI request, then use the Sanders-Casar plan once to expose the different policy mechanisms. Avoid speculative catastrophe, legislative horse-race prediction, company-motive claims and a generic contact-your-representative ending.

explanationArc.adaptation: The dated event leads; the centre compares coverage and triggers; the landing equips the reader to classify later policy claims without assigning her a monitoring job.

discoveryChecks.question: Did OpenAI create mandatory national rules?
discoveryChecks.answer: No. OpenAI asked Congress to enact them.

discoveryChecks.question: Did Sanders and Casar’s announcement establish an AI pause?
discoveryChecks.answer: No. Their office described the legislation as forthcoming.

discoveryChecks.question: Are the proposals the same?
discoveryChecks.answer: No. OpenAI proposes targeted capability-based duties for the largest labs; Sanders and Casar propose a pause until a regulator sets rules plus a permanent ban on their defined category of superintelligence.

representativeProofPlan.highestRisk: The story could turn a serious but single-firm threat report into settled attribution, confuse a Codex harness with an OpenAI model or expose operational attack detail.
representativeProofPlan.plannedProof: State the harness-versus-model distinction in one sentence and place PaperCut’s confirmation and non-verification before interpreting speed or harm.
representativeProofPlan.acceptanceOutcome: A reader can explain the AI coordination role, the vulnerable-server role, the 12-organization administrator-access limit, the vendor response and what remains unverified.
